site.markdown:
# Picking robots that work in your warehouse, not a new one

Kessler robots pick grocery orders inside existing warehouses, alongside people, with no new racking.

## The fleet

About 400 Kessler units run across customer sites today. Every robot reports to our fleet service, which schedules work, watches battery and health, and ships software updates to the fleet in waves.

## Updates without downtime

We update robots during their charging windows, a few at a time, so a warehouse never stops picking for a software release.

## Careers

We are hiring fleet software engineers in Rotterdam and Pittsburgh.

# Engineering at Kessler

## Rolling back a fleet update at 4 am

By the fleet team

In March a release changed how robots reserved aisles, and two sites saw pickers waiting on robots. This is how the fleet service noticed, how the rollback ran one site at a time, and the two checks we added before a wave can start.

## Why every robot carries its own map

By the autonomy team

A shared map sounds simpler. Here is why we stopped.

data.invite_line: Your team ships software to about 400 robots running inside other companies' warehouses, and rolled back a fleet update site by site in March. Most of our listeners are about to have that problem, and few have solved it.
data.episode_title: Shipping software to 400 robots in other people's warehouses
data.angle: We would dig into the fleet service: how updates go out in waves during charging windows, what the service watches to decide a wave is safe, and the March rollback, from the first sign that pickers were waiting on robots to the two checks you added afterwards. Then hiring: what you look for in a fleet software engineer now that the team is growing. No founding story and no product talk from our side, just the system and the calls behind it.
